title: Utilitarianism
body:
**Utilitarianism** judges an action by its consequences. The right action is the one producing
the greatest total wellbeing across everyone affected, and nothing about the action itself
matters apart from what it brings about.

It is the framework closest to how engineering decisions already get made, since a cost-benefit
analysis is a utilitarian calculation with money as the measure. Deploying a system that saves
a million hours of work and costs a hundred jobs is exactly the shape of calculation it
performs.

Two difficulties, and both come up repeatedly in the course:

**Totals hide distribution.** An outcome excellent on average can be produced by imposing
severe harm on a small group, and the arithmetic will not object. Automation that raises total
output while concentrating the loss on one occupation is the standard case, covered in
[[Automation and Job Displacement]].

**Consequences have to be predicted.** The calculation needs to know what will happen, and for
a technology deployed at scale nobody does. A recommendation system optimising engagement was a
defensible utilitarian choice on the evidence available at the time.

[[Kantianism]] is the usual counterweight, since it rules out the small-group problem by
judging the action itself and ignoring the total.
